readings.c1s1:
¶
'''awkwardness''' (âk′wärd-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being awkward. {{smaller|(''a'') Clumsiness; unwieldiness; unsuitableness: as, the ''awkwardness'' of a tool, or of a plan of operations; the ''awkwardness'' of a bundle on account of its size or shape. (''b'') Lack of skill or dexterity in action. (''c'') Lack of ease in action; ungracefulness. (''d'') An awkward circumstance or feeling; embarrassment; unpleasantness; inconvenience.}}

'''awl''' (âl), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''aul, all,'' and by misdivision (''a nawl'' for ''an awl'') ''nawl, naul, nall,'' ME. ''nal.'' The earlier forms are of four types: (1) ME. ''aule, eawle, oul,'' < AS. ''awel, awul;'' (2) ME. ''oule, ouel, owel, owul,'' < AS. ''āwel, āwul;'' (3) ME. ''el, ele,'' < AS. ''ǣl;'' (4) ME. ''alle, al,'' < AS. ''al, eal'' = OLG. ''ael'' = OHG. ''ala,'' MHG. ''ale,'' G. ''ahle'' = Icel. ''alr,'' an awl; with added formative, OHG. ''alansa, alunsa, *alasna'' (> ML. ''alesna,'' > It. ''lesina'' = Sp. ''lesna, alesna'' = Pr. ''alena'' = OF. ''alesne,'' F. ''alène'') = OD. ''aelsene, elsene'' (mod. D. ''els''), > Sc. ''elsin, elson,'' Shetland ''alison,'' an awl. Cf. Skt. ''ārā,'' an awl.] '''1.'''
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|''a'', Brad-awl; ''b'', Sewing-awl.}}}}
A pointed instrument for piercing small holes in leather, wood, etc., as the bent-pointed ''awl'' of the shoemaker and saddler and the straight-pointed ''brad-awl'' of the joiner.—'''2.''' The popinjay or green woodpecker, ''Picus'' or ''Gecinus viridis.'' [Local, British.]

'''awl-bird''' (âl′bėrd), ''n.'' Same as ''awl'', 2. ''Montagu.''

'''awl-clip''' (âl′klip), ''n.'' A device for holding blanks, memoranda, etc., consisting of an awl
readings.c1s2:
or pin fixed to a stand. The papers to be kept on file are thrust upon the pin.

'''awless''', ''a.'' See ''aweless''.

'''awl-shaped''' (âl′shāpt), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having the shape of an awl.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', slender and tapering toward the extremity from a broadish base, as a leaf; subulate.

'''awl-tree''' (âl′trē), ''n.'' [< ''awl'', repr. Hind. ''āl'' (see ''al''<sup>1</sup>, ''al-root''), + ''tree''.] Same as ''al''<sup>1</sup>.

'''awlwort''' (âl′wėrt), ''n.'' The popular name of the ''Subularia aquatica'': so called from its awl-shaped leaves (Latin ''subula'', an awl). {{smaller|It is a very small stemless aquatic plant, natural order ''Cruciferæ'', found in Europe, Siberia, and North America.}}

'''awm''' (âm), ''n.'' Same as ''aam''.

'''awmbry†''' (âm′bri), ''n.'' Same as ''ambry''.

'''awmous''' (â′mus), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''alms''.

'''awn<sup>1</sup>''' (ân), ''n.'' [E. dial. also ''ang''; < ME. ''awne'', ''aune'', ''awene'', earlier ''agun'', < AS. *''agun'' (not recorded; the ME. may be from the Scand.) = OHG. ''agana'', MHG. ''agene'', ''agne'', ''ane'', G. ''ahne'' (also ''agen''), awn, = Icel. ''ögn'', pl. ''agnar'', = Sw. ''agn'', only in pl. ''agnar'', = Dan. ''avne'' = Goth. ''ahana'', chaff, = Gr. ἄχνη, Doric ἄχνα, chaff; cf. (with diff. formative) Gr. ἄχυρον, chaff, L. ''acus'' (''acer-''), chaff, and AS. ''egl'', E. ''ail''<sup>2</sup>, awn, and AS. ''eár'' (contr. of *''ahur'' = ONorth. ''eher'', ''æhher''), E. ''ear''<sup>2</sup> (of corn) (see ''ail''<sup>2</sup>, ''avel'', ''acerose'', and ''ear''<sup>2</sup>); ult. < *''ak'', be sharp. But it is possible that two orig. different words, meaning ‘awn’ and ‘chaff’ respectively, have here run together.] In ''bot.'', a bristle-shaped terminal or dorsal appendage, such as the beard of wheat, barley,
readings.c1s3:
and many grasses.

'''awn<sup>2</sup>''', ''a.'' and ''v.'' An obsolete or dialectal form of ''own''.

'''awned''' (ând), ''a.'' [< ''awn''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Having awns: applied to leaves, leaf-stalks, etc., bearing a long rigid spine, as in barley, etc.

'''awner''' (â′nėr), ''n.'' A machine for removing the avels or awns from grain; an aveler; a hummeler. See ''hummeling-machine.''

'''awning''' (â′ning), ''n.'' [First recorded in the 17th century, in naut. use; of undetermined origin, but appar. (with suffix ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>) < *''awn'', prob. a naut. reduction of F. ''auvent'', “a penthouse of cloth before a shop-window” (Cotgrave), OF. ''auvant'', ML. ''auvanna'' (also spelled ''auventus'', appar. in simulation of L. ''ventus'', wind), of unknown origin.] A movable roof-like covering of canvas or other cloth spread over any place, or in front of a window, door, etc., as a protection from the sun’s rays.
{{smaller block|<poem>. . A court
Compact with lucid marbles, boss’d with lengths
Of classic frieze, with ample ''awnings'' gay.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}
It was very hot, and sitting under the ''awning'' turned out to be the pleasantest occupation.
{{right|''Lady Brassey'', Voyage of Sunbeam, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Backbone of an awning.''' See ''backbone.''—'''To house awnings.''' See ''house'', ''v.''}}

'''awnless''' (ân′les), ''a.'' [< ''awn''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] Without awns or beard.

'''awny''' (â′ni), ''a.'' [< ''awn''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Having awns; bearded; bristly.

readings.c2s1:
¶
'''awoke''' (a-wōk′). Preterit and past participle of ''awake''.

'''awork†''' (a-wėrk′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ME. ''awerke''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''work''.] At work; in a state of labor or action.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Twere a good mirth now to set him ''a-work''
To make her wedding-ring.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', Chaste Maid, i. 1.}}
The bad will have but small matter whereon to set their mischiefe ''a work''. {{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''aworking''' (ạ-wėr′king), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''working''.] At work; in or into a state of working or action.
{{smaller block|<poem>Never met
Adventure which might them ''a working'' set.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 224.}}}}

'''awreak†''', ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''awreken'', < AS. ''āwrecan'', < ''ā-'' + ''wrecan'', wreak: see ''a-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wreak''.] To wreak; take vengeance on; avenge.
{{smaller block|<poem>Me were lever than al this toun
Of this dispit ''awroken'' for to be.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 566.}}}}

'''awrong†''' (ạ-rông′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wrong''. Cf. ''aright'', a much older word.] In a wrong manner; wrongly.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I aim’d
''Awrong'', ’twas in an envy of thy goodness.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Lady’s Trial, iii. 3.}}}}

'''awry''' (ạ-rī′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ME. ''awry'', ''awrye'', ''on wry''; < ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wry''.] '''1.''' Turned or twisted toward one side; not in a straight or true direction or position; asquint: as, to glance or look ''awry''; the lady’s cap is ''awry''.
{{smaller block|If she steps, looks, or moves ''awry''. {{right|''Spectator'', No. 66.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
''öxa'', ax; from the noun.] To shape or trim with an ax.

'''ax<sup>2</sup>†, axe<sup>2</sup>†''' (aks), ''n.'' [< ME. ''ax'', ''axe'' (in comp.), ''ex'', ''exe'', also ''as'', < AS. ''eax'', ''æx'' = OD. ''asse'', D. ''as'' = OHG. ''ahsa'', MHG. ''ahse'', G. ''achse'' = Dan. ''axe'' = L. ''axis'' = Gr. ἄξων = OBulg. ''osĭ'', Bulg. Serv. ''os'' = Pol. ''os'' = Russ. ''osĭ'' = Lith. ''aszis'' = Skt. ''aksha'', axis, axle. Hence ''axle'', q. v.] An axle; an axis.

'''ax<sup>3</sup>, axe<sup>3</sup>''' (aks), ''v. t.'' Obsolete or dialectal forms of ''ask''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|<poem>For I wol ''axe'' if it hir wille be
To be my wyf.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer.''}}}}

'''axal''' (ak′sạl), ''a.'' Same as ''axial''.

'''axe<sup>1</sup>''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''ax''<sup>1</sup>.

'''axe<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' See ''ax''<sup>2</sup>.

'''axe<sup>3</sup>''', ''v.'' See ''ax''<sup>3</sup>.

'''axe<sup>4</sup>''' (aks), ''n.'' An English name of a native species of ''Lobelia'', ''L. urens''.

'''axed''' (akst), ''a.'' [< ''ax''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''masonry'', dressed with a stone hammer to a smooth surface.
{{smaller block|Good effect is obtained by the contrast of ''axed'' and polished surfaces.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IV. 474.}}}}

'''axes''', ''n.'' Plural of ''ax'' and of ''axis''.

'''axfitch†''', ''n.'' [Also written ''axvitch'', ''axfetch''; < ''ax''<sup>1</sup> + ''fitch''. This and the other names ''axseed'', ''axwort'', ''hatchet-fitch'', and NL. ''Securigera'', refer to the ax-shaped seed.] A leguminous plant, ''Securigera coronilla''. ''Cotgrave.''

'''ax-form''' (aks′fôrm), ''a.'' Same as ''ax-shaped''.

'''ax-head''' (aks′hed), ''n.'' The head or iron of an ax. Ancient ax-heads, formed of stone and sometimes of bronze, are called ''celts''.

''ascia'', ax, mattock, akin to Gr. ἀξίνη, ax.]   An instrument used for hewing timber and chopping wood, and also as a weapon of offense. {{smaller|The modern ax consists of a head of iron, with an arching edge of steel, and a helve or handle. The edge is in the plane of the sweep of}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0427 c2f2.png|width=195px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Ax of jadeite from New Ireland.}}}} {{smaller|the tool, thus differing from the adz, in which the edge is at right angles to the plane of the sweep. The northern nations who overthrew the Roman empire used many varieties of this weapon, and its use prevailed throughout the middle ages in Europe. A light ax was common among the Arabs and Moors. Axes of various kinds of stone, or entirely of copper or bronze, are found among prehistoric and ancient remains, and in use by barbarous races. '''ax-form''' (aks′fôrm), ''a.'' Same as ''ax-shaped''. '''ax-head''' (aks′hed), ''n.'' The head or iron of an ax. Ancient ax-heads, formed of stone and sometimes of bronze, are called ''celts''. '''axial''' (ak′si-al), ''a.''   [< ''axis'' + ''-al.'']   '''1.''' Pertaining to or of the nature of an axis. {{smaller block|From central development we pass insensibly to that higher kind of development for which ''axial'' seems the most appropriate name. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Biol., § 50.}}}} '''2.''' Situated in an axis or in the axis.—'''3.''' In ''anat.'', pertaining to the somatic as distinguished from the membral portions of the body; not appendicular. {{smaller|Axial parts or organs are, in general, divided into ''epaxial'', ''hypaxial'', and ''paraxial'', according as they are situated over, under, or alongside the spinal column.}} '''4.''' In ''geol.'', forming the axis, central dominating portion, or crest of a mountain-range. Sometimes ''axal.'' {{smaller|'''Axial canal''', in crinoids, the central canal within the hard perisoma of the stem, extending the length of the latter and filled with a soft solid substance.—'''Axial cavity''', in ''Actinozoa'', the cavity common to the gastric sac and intermesenteric chambers. See ''Actinozoa''.—'''Axial circle''', a circle having its center on the axis of a curve.—'''Axial line''', the name given by Faraday to the line in which the magnetic force passes from one pole of a horseshoe magnet to the other.—'''Axial plane''', in ''crystal.'', a plane containing (1) two of the crystallographic axes, or (2) the optic axes in the case of a biaxial crystal.—'''Axial rotation''', rotation upon an axis.—'''Axial skeleton''', the skeleton of the trunk and head and tail, as distinct from the skeleton of the limbs.}} [[File:century v01 p0427 c3f1.png|center|302px]] {{c|{{smaller|Section of mountain showing anticlinal structure with axial mass of eruptive or metamorphic rock.}}}} {{smaller block|The central or axial portions of many mountain-ranges consist of crystalline, azoic, or archæan rocks; this is especially true of the numerous ranges of the North American Cordilleras.}} '''axially''' (ak′si-a̤l-i), ''adv.''
